newsitem.title: UK: Russia eyes seven-year maturity for mark Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Russia eyes seven-year maturity for mark Eurobond.

text.p: Russia's debut mark Eurobond, due to be launched in early March, was likely to have a maturity of up to seven years, bankers said on Monday.
"The mark bond is likely to have a five- to seven-year maturity," an official at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.
Russia's deputy finance minister Mikhail Kasyanov said on Monday a 1.0 billion mark ($610 million) Eurobond was planned for early March via Credit Suisse First Boston and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The deal would be the first of a $3.0 billion fundraising programme expected in 1997, he said.

Russia tapped the international capital markets for the first time since its 1917 revolution last November with a $1.0 billion five-year bond. Launched to yield 345 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes, the deal was heavily oversubscribed.

"The Russians will be interested in maturity extension," a banker involved in the dollar Eurobond said. "The mark sector, for high-yielding borrowers, has provided long maturities. For example, Argentina issued 30-year paper last year."
"Given mark spreads often come tight to dollar spreads, the dollar spread of 345 b.p. would be an absolute ceiling for a seven-year mark bond," he said.
The deal could come even tighter, dealers said, reflecting retail investor appetite for high yields.
"If you have really good pre-marketing, like with Russia's dollar Eurobond, the mark deal will go very well," a syndicate manager at a European bank in Frankfurt said.
"Investors are really greedy for yield and also for the name. They are looking for new names in the Euromark sector."
The Deutsche official said: "A lot of retail investors will buy this paper as they are after high-yielders and this would be in the high-yielder group."
"The high coupon really appeals to retail...triple-A rated borrowers hardly pay a five percent coupon."
Russia's dollar bond was mainly driven by institutional demand, and these investors would also participate in the mark issue, although to a lesser extent.
"Retail demand will be a significant factor but not the sole driving factor," a trader familiar with the mark deal said.

"Institutional demand will be substantial because of the size and the rarity value. We have done a number of private placements for Eastern European borrowers and have seen phenomenal demand out of Asia, especially Korea."
Russian debt rallied on Monday on news of the Eurobond and on plans Russia would reschedule London Club debt by the end of March or early April.
Its 2001 dollar global was trading at 340 b.p. over U.S. Treasury notes and dollar-denominated MinFin bonds also rallied.
Continued uncertainty about the state of President Boris Yeltsin's health was not worrying the market.
